QueryGuard: A Safety Gate
An intro to why LLM-generated SQL needs a validation gate, the gap in existing defenses, and the QueryGuard pipeline. We outline our two-member workstreams, the planned evaluation, and the course roadmap ahead.
Notes
Welcome everyone. Today we present QueryGuard, a safety gate for LLM-generated SQL. We will explain why a validation gate is needed, the gap in existing defenses, and how our pipeline works. Mahd and Arwa each lead a workstream, and we close with our planned evaluation and the course roadmap.
Slide 2
1/27/13
2
The Problem: Unguarded LLM SQL
Applications let users query databases in plain English, and frameworks pass LLM-generated SQL straight to the database with no review layer in between.
Notes
This slide frames the threat landscape. Users type plain-English questions, frameworks forward LLM-generated SQL directly to databases, and real CVEs show the consequences: Vanna AI remote code execution at CVSS 8.1, LlamaIndex NL2SQL exploitation at 9.8, and AnythingLLM data extraction at 7.7. We close with the research baseline that 96 percent of manual prompt-injection attacks succeed against undefended pipelines, which motivates our planned evaluation.
Slide 3
1/27/13
3
Defenses & the Gap
Model-side fixes like StruQ and SecAlign require retraining or fine-tuning, while generic guardrails such as NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails and Guardrails AI are schema-unaware and opaque. QueryGuard plans a transparent, deterministic, SQL-specific check between LLM and database.
Notes
This slide explains why a new layer of defense is needed. Model-side fixes such as StruQ and SecAlign demand retraining or fine-tuning, which is costly and inflexible. Generic guardrails like NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails and Guardrails AI operate as opaque, schema-unaware classifiers. Neither offers a transparent, deterministic, SQL-specific check. QueryGuard is planned to occupy exactly this position, at the application layer between the LLM and the database.
Slide 4
1/27/13
4
QueryGuard Pipeline
1
Intake Stage
Incoming requests enter one transparent entry point, so every query follows a single recorded path.
2
Generator Stage
A candidate SQL query is produced by the LLM or by a deterministic mock, keeping generation swappable.
3
Validation Gate
Every candidate query is checked against fixed rules before anything is allowed to move further.
4
Executor Boundary
Only gate-passed queries run; the read-only trust boundary is architectural, not advisory.
5
Audit Log
All outcomes are written to an append-only audit log, giving a complete, inspectable record.
Notes
This slide presents our planned QueryGuard solution as a five-stage pipeline at the application layer. Queries enter through intake, are generated by the LLM or a deterministic mock, and must pass the validation gate. Only gate-passed queries reach the read-only executor, and every outcome lands in the append-only audit log. Because the trust boundary is architectural rather than advisory, no query can bypass the gate, and each stage stays inspectable for review.
Slide 5
1/27/13
5
Inside the Validation Gate
10 deterministic rules check each generated query, so enforcement relies on architecture rather than model behavior.
PASS or BLOCK Verdict
Each query receives PASS or BLOCK, together with the specific rule that fired, as planned.
Sensitive Columns MASKED
Sensitive columns are MASKED in the plan, keeping private data out of anything that executes.
Missing Limits SUGGESTED
Queries missing row limits get SUGGESTED additions, tightening safety before execution.
Notes
Inside the validation gate, ten deterministic rules evaluate every generated query before it moves forward. Each query exits with a PASS or BLOCK verdict plus the specific rule that fired, sensitive columns can be MASKED, and missing limits are SUGGESTED. The read-only executor accepts only gate-passed queries, so enforcement depends on architecture rather than on the model behaving well.

Evaluation Plan
100%
Target block rate on destructive attack classes, to be validated against the 30-prompt attack corpus in planned evaluation work.
<10%
False positive ceiling on the 30 benign prompts; results will be reported openly once the evaluation run is completed as planned.
<50ms
Target p95 added latency for the SQL security gate, measured during the planned evaluation rather than claimed from completed runs.
Notes
This slide frames evaluation as planned work, not finished results. The corpus holds 30 attack and 30 benign prompts across six published attack classes. Targets: full blocking of destructive classes, false positives under ten percent reported openly, p95 added gate latency under fifty milliseconds, and zero silent regressions, since the corpus runs in continuous integration and a broken rule fails the build. All figures are targets; evaluation has not yet been run.

Course, Milestones, Stack
Two-Member Team
CS 5391 Software Engineering group project carried out by M. Mahd Amjad and Arwa Arafeh.
Milestone Plan
Proposal and presentation first, then an SRS with numbered requirements mapped to test cases.

pytest and CI

Mock LLM Mode
A mock LLM mode keeps demos deterministic; a live LLM integration remains optional.
Final Demo
Implementation and demo round out the milestone schedule ahead of the final.
Notes

We review the milestone order — proposal and presentation, an SRS whose numbered requirements map to test cases, then implementation and demo before the final — and the stack: Flask, a SQLite database with deliberately sensitive columns for our planned evaluation, pytest with GitHub Actions CI, and a mock LLM mode that keeps demos deterministic.
